thread_title: S. leucophylla, Washington Co, AL (2014 update)
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla, Washington Co, AL (2014 update)

posts.body_html:
Beautiful plants. Mike, what can you tell me about the nature of the rhizomes of these wild populations? Naturally everyone visiting them focusses on the pitchers (at least in picture taking) but rarely speaks on the plants' foundations.

Say in leucs like these, how are the rhizomes situated as relates to ground level? By that I mean, are they half in/half out of the soil as per typical cultivation process; fully under the soil; or, as I suspect, in a variety of positions?

What is the state of the remnant prior seasons pitchers (the dead stuff) at that rhizome level? Is it completely degraded away or remaining like up turned fingers?

Are there many new growth points along the rhizomes?

I know these are questions that may have obvious answers; but then again they may not. I'm just trying to get a handle on how our horticultural practices, sometimes forcing techniques in essence which are very successful in propagating much new growth, actually relate to the natural behaviour of the wild specimens. And, I understand they would be hard to view with all the foliage of other local flora, but is there anything you can tell us?

posts.body_html:
Great questions KE! I too was very curious about the rhizome, but my interest was mainly in the growth points.

As for the previous year's traps, many had toppled over. The phyllodia from the previous year was still in tact on many plants, but it was completely brown. As far as growth points are concerned, you don't see 6-7 heads all closely crowded together like you do in cultivated plants. Instead, you see 6-7 LONG rhizomes "running" in different directions. Very few of these have any branching "heads."

As far as their position in the ground, it's exactly the same as you'd see in cultivation: the top of the "back" is exposed, but the rest is covered in soil. Of course, plants that had been blasted out of the soil, covered in soil,etc. from the weather were in abnormal positions, but that was an exception to the rule. I didn't see many in other positions.

I was curious about fall pitcher production because I wanted to see if there's a way to predict whether or not you're going to have a good fall flush of pitchers. Here's what I observed in the wild:
1) In August, a few plants that already had 2-3 fall pitchers had dormant growth points.
2) In rhizomes that hadn't yet produced fall pitchers, you could see new ones emerging and still growing.
3) In very few instances, you could find plants that had 2-3 fall pitchers, but still have 1-2 new ones forming. That was almost non-existent, the maximum I counted was 4 fall pitchers on one growth point. If I had to guess, the average was 1-2 fall pitchers per growth point, but many clones had multiple heads, so without seeing the details, it looks as though each growth point is pushing out a lot of traps.

Not sure what you want to know about the foliage of other surrounding plants? Unfortunately, I didn't pay very close attention to them, except a few of the outstanding species (Sabatia, Lilium, etc).

posts.body_html:
I'm not too sure, we didn't pay much close attention to the rhizomes, but it appeared there weren't many plants that had side buds on the rhizomes. However, I did see some main growth points splitting into 2 new growth points...was that more frequent than side shoots forming? I'm not sure, but I would suspect growth patterns differ from one site to the next.

Indeed, it was difficult to see the rhizomes at most of the sites because they're typically densely covered with surrounding growth. You definitely have to clear away stuff to see the rhizomes, so what we saw was a small sample of everything. Our observations aren't the best measure.

Anyhow, some more photos!



While I've seen more brighter white S. leucophyllas in other locations, I don't think I've ever seen so many alba or alba-like clones in a field of equal size and density:


Love how the white travels down the traps. In cultivation, immature traps don't typically express this phenotype; usually, the traps have to be pretty big in order to get that much white to show up:















Water stress? Not sure:


Now this one, I'm 90% sure has a wilting lid due to water stress:



and Gosh, ain't it a beauty?
















Alright, that's it for this one site! I have more photos from another washington Co, AL site that's actually relatively far away from this one but the plants look very similar, so stay tuned!

posts.body_html:
Haha KE totally - no two alike and each lovely in its own way. 

I was surprised at the unbranched length on many Sarr rhizomes in the wild - much longer than typically seen in cultivation as Mike said. In areas where the soil was bare some plants had 2 feet or so of back rhizome snaking along the ground. The Sandy Creek (Bay Co.) flavas seemed like reluctant clumpers and no doubt we would have found long back rhizomes on them if we had gone digging through the grass. There was a Liberty Co. flava ornata genet I posted a pic of 6-8 feet across but with only 6-8 growth points, indicating little branching. Then on the other hand there were clones that formed incredibly dense masses of growth points, often times growing right next to sparsely branched plants. The "Outlaw" ornata comes to mind - clearly a clumper. So in short I think it's genetics, with some populations having a mix of branchers and non-branchers, and some even having mostly or all non-branchers. In cultivation we don't grow our plants with competing grasses etc. so more light reaches the rhizome and activates dormant eyes. Plus we tend to select for clumping vigor and often toss (and are less likely to receive via division) those plants that are exceptionally slow to multiply!

posts.body_html:
Thanks for sharing your observations Calen! the outlaw site is rather unique in the sense that it seems as though the owners are mowing and harvesting hay from the field. Did the plants seem shorter in that field than in other populations you visited? If so, that would imply that the hay was harvested during the grow season. That would also imply the plants had their pitchers chopped off during the grow season, which means you have a larger ratio of roots to shoots. Under such circumstances, since auxins are mostly produced in the root tips and shoot tips, the plant is no longer balanced hormonally, and you'll have a larger ratio of auxin to cytokinin. As a result, the plant triggers more growth points to compensate for the hormonal imbalance, which may explain why the outlaw site is more clumpy than other sites.

Is that nerded out enough?

posts.body_html:
meizzwang your nerd-fu is impressive indeed. You are unquestionably a super-nerd, which is of course a big compliment in present company
You may well be dead right Mike. Yes, I think they harvest hay, and yes the plants were shorter than average. The site was dryish when we visited and water stress was our initial hypothesis. But then Trey went back to the site 6 weeks later and he was sloshing through standing water (though they still hadnt cut any hay either). So clearly the water table varies quite a bit (growers take note!) and depends to a large extent on storm events. So that kinda casts doubt on our water stress theory. Overall I wouldn't say that the plants there were unaccountably clumpy - many were single or only a few growth points - and "the" outlaw clone was definitely an outlier. But if they cut hay, which they would probably do in August when the field is at it's vegetative peak (and after, incidentally, flava has done much of it's business for the season), I agree that could tend to "stunt" the plants and likely encourage lateral budding. Trey and I plan to return to the area and we should be able to gather more information about the genetics and environmental conditions. You can be sure we will keep the forum updated
